tanstack-query.title: 01. What is the difference between Server State and Client State, and why does TanStack Query exist?
tanstack-query.content: Client state is synchronous and owned by the browser, whereas server state is asynchronous, shared, remotely persisted, and potentially stale—requiring caching, deduplication, and background synchronization.

blocks.text:
• Client State: Synchronous, local to the session (theme, modal open/close, form draft). You own the single source of truth.
• Server State: Persisted remotely (database/API), fetched asynchronously, mutated by other users/processes, and becomes stale the moment it arrives.
• Why TanStack Query? Using Redux or useEffect for API data forces you to hand-write caching, request deduplication, race-condition guards, retries, and background revalidation. TanStack Query is an async state manager purpose-built for that lifecycle.

tanstack-query.title: 02. What is the role of QueryClient and QueryClientProvider, and why should QueryClient not be created inside a render body?
tanstack-query.content: QueryClient holds the QueryCache, MutationCache, and default configuration; creating it inside a component render without memoization wipes the entire cache on re-renders.

blocks.text:
• QueryClient Role: It orchestrates QueryCache and MutationCache, manages active observers, deduplicates in-flight requests, and exposes imperative methods (invalidateQueries, prefetchQuery, setQueryData).
• QueryClientProvider: Distributes the QueryClient instance via React Context to all hooks.
• Render Pitfall: Instantiating `new QueryClient()` directly inside a component body recreates a brand-new empty cache on every render. Create it at module scope in SPAs, or inside `useState(() => new QueryClient())` / per-request factory in SSR.

tanstack-query.title: 03. Explain staleTime vs. gcTime (formerly cacheTime) in TanStack Query v5.
tanstack-query.content: staleTime controls how long cached data is considered fresh before triggering background refetches; gcTime controls how long unused (inactive) cached data stays in memory before garbage collection.

blocks.text:
• staleTime (default: 0): While data is fresh, components mounting with the same queryKey read immediately from cache without network refetching. Once staleTime elapses, cached data is still shown immediately, but background refetches trigger on mount, window focus, or reconnect.
• gcTime (default: 5 minutes, renamed from cacheTime in v5): The countdown starts only when a query has zero active observers (all subscribed components unmount). When gcTime expires, the cache entry is garbage-collected.
• Rule of Thumb: Always keep `gcTime >= staleTime` so fresh data is not prematurely evicted.

tanstack-query.title: 04. How do queryKeys work internally, and how does object vs. array ordering affect cache hits?
tanstack-query.content: queryKeys must be arrays and are serialized deterministically: array element order is significant, whereas plain object property order inside a key is normalized and identical.

blocks.text:
• Array-Only in v4/v5: Every queryKey is an array (`['users', id, filters]`) which enables hierarchical prefix matching during invalidation.
• Deterministic Hashing: TanStack Query serializes keys with `hashKey`, sorting object keys alphabetically. Thus `{ status: 'done', page: 1 }` and `{ page: 1, status: 'done' }` map to the exact same cache entry.
• Array Position Matters: `['todos', 1, 2]` and `['todos', 2, 1]` are distinct cache entries.
• Dependencies Rule: Include every variable used inside `queryFn` in `queryKey` so changing parameters automatically switches cache slots and refetches.

tanstack-query.title: 05. How does request deduplication work when multiple components mount with the same queryKey simultaneously?
tanstack-query.content: TanStack Query attaches multiple QueryObservers to a single Query instance in QueryCache, sharing one in-flight Promise and firing only a single network request.

blocks.text:
• Single Query, Multiple Observers: Each `useQuery` call creates a `QueryObserver` subscribed to the `Query` entry identified by the hashed `queryKey`.
• In-Flight Sharing: If a fetch is already in progress (`fetchStatus === 'fetching'`), subsequent components mounting with the same key join the existing Promise instead of firing duplicate HTTP calls.
• Independent Options: Each observer can still specify its own `select` or `notifyOnChangeProps` while sharing the underlying cache entry.

tanstack-query.title: 06. Which automatic events trigger background refetches by default, and how does staleTime gate them?
tanstack-query.content: By default, TanStack Query refetches on component mount, window focus, and network reconnection—but only when the cached data is stale (unless set to 'always').

blocks.text:
• Default Triggers:
  1. New observer mounts (`refetchOnMount`).
  2. Browser window/tab regains focus (`refetchOnWindowFocus`).
  3. Network reconnects (`refetchOnReconnect`).
  4. Periodic timer (`refetchInterval`, disabled by default).
• Role of `staleTime`: If data is still fresh, none of the first three triggers fire a request.
• Special Values: Setting `refetchOnMount: 'always'` forces a refetch regardless of `staleTime`, whereas `false` disables the trigger completely.

tanstack-query.title: 07. Why is checking response.ok critical when using native fetch() with TanStack Query?
tanstack-query.content: Native fetch() only rejects on network failures and resolves on HTTP 404/500 responses; without throwing on `!res.ok`, TanStack Query treats error responses as successful data.

blocks.text:
• Fetch Behavior vs. Axios: Axios automatically rejects Promises on non-2xx statuses, whereas `fetch()` resolves normally on HTTP 400, 401, 404, or 500.
• Impact in TanStack Query: If `queryFn` does not throw, TanStack Query sets `status: 'success'`, caches the error JSON as valid `data`, and never triggers `retry` or `error` boundaries.
• Best Practice: Wrap `fetch` in a tiny helper that throws a typed `HttpError(res.status, body)` whenever `!res.ok`.

tanstack-query.title: 08. How does TanStack Query retry failed queries by default, and how should you customize retry for 4xx client errors?
tanstack-query.content: Queries retry 3 times with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s capped at 30s), while mutations default to 0 retries; pass a function to `retry` to skip retrying 401/403/404 errors.

blocks.text:
• Default Behavior: `useQuery` retries 3 times on the client (0 on SSR to avoid slowing server responses), using `Math.min(1000 * 2 ** attemptIndex, 30000)`. `useMutation` does NOT retry by default (`retry: 0`).
• Skipping Deterministic Errors: Retrying a 404 Not Found or 401 Unauthorized wastes 7+ seconds before showing an error UI. Inspect `error.status` inside `retry(failureCount, error)` and return `false` immediately for client 4xx errors.

tanstack-query.title: 09. How do you build a global background-fetching indicator while excluding noisy polling queries?
tanstack-query.content: Use `useIsFetching(filters)` with a `queryKey` prefix or `predicate` function to exclude periodic background polls from triggering your global loading bar.

blocks.text:
• `useIsFetching()`: Without arguments, returns the total count of currently fetching queries across the whole `QueryClient`.
• Filtering Noise: Passing a `predicate` (or `queryKey`) lets you ignore silent polling queries like `['notifications']` or `['heartbeat']` so users aren't distracted by a flickering top progress bar every few seconds.

tanstack-query.title: 10. What is the idiomatic way to build a debounced search input with TanStack Query?
tanstack-query.content: Debounce the input value before placing it into `queryKey`, pass `signal` for cancellation, gate short inputs with `enabled`, and optionally preserve prior results with `placeholderData: keepPreviousData`.

blocks.text:
• Debounce State, Not `queryFn`: Debouncing inside `queryFn` breaks TanStack Query's Promise tracking and key-based caching. Instead, store a debounced state (`debouncedQuery`) and put it in `queryKey`.
• Bonus Optimizations:
  - Cached results for previously typed terms appear instantaneously.
  - Passing `signal` aborts superseded requests if the user types again after 300ms.
  - `placeholderData: keepPreviousData` avoids flashing an empty list between keystrokes.

tanstack-query.title: 11. When should you use `staleTime: Infinity`, and how does it still allow manual refreshes?
tanstack-query.content: `staleTime: Infinity` prevents automatic background refetches (mount, focus, reconnect) for static/rarely changing data, while `invalidateQueries()` or `refetch()` can still refresh it explicitly.

blocks.text:
• Ideal Use Cases: Country lists, static enums, feature-flag snapshots, or WebSocket-pushed caches where HTTP polling isn't desired.
• Does `Infinity` Freeze Forever? No! Calling `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['countries'] })` explicitly marks the entry stale and refetches it, and `refetch()` always bypasses `staleTime`.

tanstack-query.title: 12. What can you inspect with ReactQueryDevtools, and is it automatically tree-shaken in production builds?
tanstack-query.content: ReactQueryDevtools inspects live query statuses (fresh, fetching, stale, inactive), timelines, observer counts, and manual refetch/invalidate triggers; by default it is excluded from production bundles.

blocks.text:
• Inspection Capabilities: View exact serialized `queryKey`s, `dataUpdatedAt` timestamps, raw JSON cache payloads, active observer counts, and manually simulate Error, Loading, Invalidate, or Reset states.
• Bundle Size: `@tanstack/react-query-devtools` automatically compiles to `null` when `NODE_ENV === 'production'`. If you want it in production for staff debugging, use `@tanstack/react-query-devtools/production` with `React.lazy`.

tanstack-query.title: 13. What is the exact difference between refetchOnMount: true, refetchOnMount: false, and refetchOnMount: 'always'?
tanstack-query.content: refetchOnMount: true (default) refetches on mount only if cached data is stale; false never refetches on mount if cached data exists; 'always' forces a background refetch on every mount regardless of staleTime.

blocks.text:
• `true` (Default): Checks `query.isStale()`. If `staleTime` has not elapsed, mounting a component reads straight from `QueryCache` with zero network traffic.
• `false`: If the query already has data in cache (even if stale!), mounting a new observer will NOT trigger a fetch. (Note: if the query has NO data in cache yet, it still performs the initial fetch).
• `'always'`: Ignores `staleTime` (except `'static'`) and unconditionally triggers a background refetch every time a new `QueryObserver` mounts—ideal for financial balances or real-time seat availability.

tanstack-query.title: 14. How do status and fetchStatus differ in TanStack Query v5, and what changed between isPending and isLoading?
tanstack-query.content: status ('pending' | 'error' | 'success') tracks whether data exists in cache, while fetchStatus ('fetching' | 'paused' | 'idle') tracks whether queryFn is currently running. In v5, isLoading is an alias for isPending && isFetching.

blocks.text:
• Two Orthogonal Axes:
  - `status`: Describes the data (`pending` = no data yet, `error`, `success`).
  - `fetchStatus`: Describes the async `queryFn` (`fetching`, `paused` when offline, `idle`).
• Why Both? A disabled query (`enabled: false`) has `status: 'pending'` (no data) AND `fetchStatus: 'idle'` (not fetching). A background refresh has `status: 'success'` AND `fetchStatus: 'fetching'`.
• v5 Naming Change: `status: 'loading'` was renamed to `'pending'` (`isPending`), and `isLoading` now strictly means `isPending && isFetching` (replacing v4's `isInitialLoading`).

tanstack-query.title: 15. What is Structural Sharing in TanStack Query, when does it help, and when should you disable it?
tanstack-query.content: Structural sharing recursively diffs newly fetched JSON data against the previous cache entry and keeps identical object/array references intact to avoid unnecessary React re-renders.

blocks.text:
• How It Works: When a background refetch returns a fresh JSON payload where 9 of 10 items are unchanged, `replaceEqualDeep` reuses the exact old references for unchanged subtrees and only creates new references along modified paths.
• Benefits: Downstream `React.memo`, `useMemo`, and `useEffect` dependencies remain referentially stable.
• When to Disable (`structuralSharing: false`): Disable it for huge payloads (tens of thousands of rows) where deep diffing costs more CPU than rendering, or when `queryFn` returns non-JSON values (like `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, or class instances) unless you pass a custom comparator function.

tanstack-query.title: 16. How does the select option optimize performance, and why should the selector function be stabilized?
tanstack-query.content: select transforms or slices cached data per observer and prevents re-renders if the derived result is unchanged, provided the selector reference is stable (module-level or useCallback).

blocks.text:
• Per-Observer Transformation: The raw API response remains intact in `QueryCache` for other components, while each observer transforms only what it needs.
• Render Bailout: TanStack Query compares the previous and next `select` outputs (using structural sharing); if the selected primitive or slice didn't change, the component does not re-render even when unrelated fields in the cache updated.
• Stability Rule: An inline arrow function creates a new function reference on every render, forcing `select` to re-run on every render. Define selectors outside the component or wrap them with `useCallback`.

tanstack-query.title: 17. What problem does queryOptions() solve in TanStack Query v5?
tanstack-query.content: queryOptions() binds a queryKey and queryFn together with full TypeScript inference so hooks and imperative QueryClient methods share one type-safe source of truth.

blocks.text:
• Key/Fn Coupling: Defining `queryKey` and `queryFn` separately invites mismatches and forces manual generic annotations on `getQueryData<User>(['users', id])`.
• Tagged Query Keys (`DataTag`): `queryOptions()` attaches the inferred return type directly onto the `queryKey` tuple via a phantom symbol.
• End-to-End Reuse: Passing `userQueryOptions(id)` to `useQuery`, `useSuspenseQuery`, `prefetchQuery`, `ensureQueryData`, and `.queryKey` to `getQueryData` or `setQueryData` automatically infers the exact `TData` and `TError` types.

tanstack-query.title: 18. How do you implement dependent queries, and when should you prefer skipToken over enabled: false?
tanstack-query.content: Dependent queries wait on prerequisite data using `enabled: Boolean(dep)` or v5's `skipToken`; `skipToken` eliminates non-null assertions by narrowing types inside `queryFn`.

blocks.text:
• Sequential Fetching: Pass `enabled: !!user?.id` so the second query stays `pending` & `idle` until `user.id` resolves.
• TypeScript Gap with `enabled`: TypeScript cannot narrow `userId` inside `queryFn` based on the sibling `enabled` boolean, often forcing `userId!`.
• `skipToken` Advantage: Assigning `queryFn: userId ? () => fetchProjects(userId) : skipToken` disables execution while letting TypeScript narrow `userId` to `string` cleanly.
• Caveat: Unlike `enabled: false`, queries using `skipToken` cannot be imperatively triggered with `refetch()`.

tanstack-query.title: 19. How do you execute dynamic parallel queries without violating React's Rules of Hooks, and what does combine do?
tanstack-query.content: Use `useQueries` to run a variable-length array of queries in parallel, and use v5's `combine` option to aggregate results and limit re-renders.

blocks.text:
• Why Not `ids.map(() => useQuery(...))`? Calling hooks inside loops violates React's Rules of Hooks whenever `ids.length` changes.
• `useQueries`: Accepts a dynamic `queries` array and returns an array of query results executed concurrently.
• v5 `combine` Option: Reduces the array of observer results into a single derived object (e.g., merged data + combined loading flag). Combined with structural sharing, it prevents unnecessary re-renders when intermediate results match.

tanstack-query.title: 20. What is the key architectural difference between initialData and placeholderData?
tanstack-query.content: initialData is persisted into the QueryCache (and respects staleTime), whereas placeholderData is observer-only temporary UI data that never writes to the cache.

blocks.text:
• `initialData`: Seeded directly into `QueryCache` as real data (`status: 'success'`). If `staleTime > 0`, it prevents an immediate background fetch. Ideal for SSR seeding or extracting an item from a cached list.
• `placeholderData`: Exists solely at the `QueryObserver` level (`isPlaceholderData: true`) while the real query remains `fetching`. It is never saved to cache and is ideal for `keepPreviousData` during pagination or showing skeleton partial previews.

tanstack-query.title: 21. How do you configure conditional polling, and how does TanStack Query handle hidden browser tabs?
tanstack-query.content: Pass a callback to `refetchInterval` returning milliseconds or `false` to stop polling dynamically; by default, polling pauses automatically when the tab is backgrounded.

blocks.text:
• Dynamic `refetchInterval`: In v5, the callback receives the `Query` object (`query.state.data`), allowing you to stop polling once a background job finishes (`return false`).
• Tab Visibility Optimization: `refetchIntervalInBackground` defaults to `false`, pausing timers when `document.visibilityState === 'hidden'` to save battery and server load.
• Error Backoff: Consider checking `query.state.error` inside the callback to pause or slow down polling on server failures.

tanstack-query.title: 22. How does automatic query cancellation work with AbortSignal, and when does TanStack Query trigger it?
tanstack-query.content: TanStack Query passes an AbortSignal in QueryFunctionContext; forwarding it to fetch/axios aborts in-flight HTTP requests when all observers unmount or queryClient.cancelQueries() is called.

blocks.text:
• Context `signal`: Every `queryFn` receives `{ queryKey, signal, meta }`.
• When It Aborts:
  1. A component unmounts (or `queryKey` changes, e.g., fast search typing) before the promise resolves AND the `signal` was consumed by your code.
  2. You explicitly call `queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey })` (common inside `onMutate`).
• Important Note: Calling `fetch(url, { signal })` cancels the browser request cleanly and avoids wasted bandwidth and stale responses.

tanstack-query.title: 23. Compare mutate() vs. mutateAsync() in useMutation, including error handling and callback execution.
tanstack-query.content: mutate() catches errors internally and routes them to mutation state and callbacks, while mutateAsync() returns a raw Promise that rejects on failure and requires try/catch.

blocks.text:
• `mutate`: Synchronous trigger that never throws an unhandled rejection. Handle outcomes via `useMutation` callbacks (`onSuccess`, `onError`, `onSettled`) or per-call options `mutate(vars, { onSuccess })`.
• `mutateAsync`: Returns a `Promise<TData>`, useful when chaining sequential awaits or integrating with form libraries expecting a Promise. Always wrap in `try/catch`.
• Callback Pitfall: Callbacks on `useMutation({ onSuccess })` run even if the component unmounts, whereas callbacks passed to `mutate(vars, { onSuccess })` only run if the component is still mounted.

tanstack-query.title: 24. Where should cache invalidation live vs. UI redirects in useMutation, and why return the invalidateQueries promise?
tanstack-query.content: Put cache invalidation inside useMutation's callbacks (survives unmount) and UI side effects inside mutate()'s callbacks; returning the invalidateQueries promise keeps isPending true until data refreshes.

blocks.text:
• Lifecycle Separation:
  - `useMutation({ onSuccess })`: Runs regardless of whether the triggering component is still mounted—ideal for `invalidateQueries` or `setQueryData`.
  - `mutate(vars, { onSuccess })`: Skipped if the component unmounts mid-flight—ideal for `navigate()`, closing modals, or local toast messages.
• Awaiting Invalidation: Returning `queryClient.invalidateQueries(...)` from `useMutation`'s `onSuccess` makes the mutation stay `isPending` until the invalidated queries finish refetching.

tanstack-query.title: 25. Compare invalidateQueries, refetchQueries, resetQueries, and setQueryData.
tanstack-query.content: invalidateQueries marks queries stale and refetches active ones; refetchQueries forces fetching; resetQueries restores initial/empty state; setQueryData writes synchronously to cache.

blocks.text:
• `invalidateQueries`: Marks matching queries stale (`isStale = true`) and refetches active ones in the background. Inactive queries will refetch next time they mount.
• `refetchQueries`: Immediately triggers fetching for matching queries (defaults to all, or filter with `type: 'active'`).
• `resetQueries`: Resets cached data back to `initialData` (or `undefined`) before refetching active observers—helpful on logout or full filter resets.
• `setQueryData`: Synchronously and immutably updates cached data with zero network calls; never mutate the `old` reference in place.

tanstack-query.title: 26. How does QueryFilters matching work in TanStack Query (prefix vs. exact vs. predicate)?
tanstack-query.content: QueryClient methods match queryKeys by prefix by default; `exact: true` restricts to identical keys, and `predicate` runs custom filtering logic across Query instances.

blocks.text:
• Prefix Matching (Default): `{ queryKey: ['todos'] }` matches `['todos']`, `['todos', 'list']`, and `['todos', { done: true }]`.
• `exact: true`: Matches only `['todos']` with identical length and values.
• `predicate`: Receives the full `Query` instance (`queryKey`, `state`, `meta`), letting you invalidate e.g. all queries older than a timestamp or matching nested conditions.
• Additional Filters: `type: 'active' | 'inactive' | 'all'` and `stale: true | false` narrow which cached entries are targeted.

tanstack-query.title: 27. When should you use standard paginated useQuery vs. useInfiniteQuery, and what changed in v5 for useInfiniteQuery?
tanstack-query.content: Use `useQuery` with `placeholderData: keepPreviousData` for numbered page navigation, and `useInfiniteQuery` for additive feeds ('Load More' / infinite scroll); v5 requires `initialPageParam`.

blocks.text:
• Standard Pagination (`useQuery`): Each page has its own `['items', page]` cache key. Keeping previous data avoids layout jumps between page clicks.
• Infinite Queries (`useInfiniteQuery`): Accumulates all fetched pages in `data.pages` and `data.pageParams` under one cache entry.
• v5 Changes:
  1. `initialPageParam` is now mandatory (removed implicit `undefined`).
  2. `maxPages` lets you cap memory by sliding a window of pages.
  3. `getPreviousPageParam` works seamlessly with `maxPages` for bi-directional scrolling.

tanstack-query.title: 28. Why do you need QueryErrorResetBoundary when resetting an ErrorBoundary around failing queries?
tanstack-query.content: Resetting a React ErrorBoundary alone only re-renders the failing child, which immediately reads the same cached error; QueryErrorResetBoundary clears query error states so they refetch on retry.

blocks.text:
• The Retry Loop Problem: When `throwOnError: true` or `useSuspenseQuery` throws, the error remains stored in `QueryCache`. Clicking 'Retry' inside `ErrorBoundary` re-renders the component, sees the same cached error, and throws again immediately.
• Solution: `QueryErrorResetBoundary` (or `useQueryErrorResetBoundary().reset`) marks queries inside that boundary to reset and refetch when `ErrorBoundary`'s `onReset` callback executes.

tanstack-query.title: 29. Compare prefetchQuery, fetchQuery, and ensureQueryData.
tanstack-query.content: prefetchQuery never throws and returns void; fetchQuery returns data and throws on error when stale; ensureQueryData returns cached data immediately if present (even if stale unless revalidateIfStale is set) or fetches it.

blocks.text:
• `prefetchQuery`: Best for hover/intent prefetching. Resolves to `void` and catches errors internally so unhandled rejections don't crash UI.
• `fetchQuery`: Checks `staleTime`; if stale or missing, fetches and returns `TData` or throws on error.
• `ensureQueryData`: Ideal for route loaders and server utilities—returns existing cached `TData` synchronously if present (or fetches if missing), guaranteeing data availability.

tanstack-query.title: 30. Explain the three networkMode options ('online', 'always', 'offlineFirst') and how they interact with fetchStatus.
tanstack-query.content: 'online' (default) pauses queries/mutations when offline; 'always' ignores network status (useful for AsyncStorage/IndexedDB); 'offlineFirst' runs the first request and pauses retries until reconnected.

blocks.text:
• `'online'` (Default): If the browser is offline, `fetchStatus` switches to `'paused'`, delaying execution and retries until the `online` event fires.
• `'always'`: Executes regardless of `navigator.onLine`—essential when `queryFn` reads IndexedDB, Electron IPC, or localhost services.
• `'offlineFirst'`: Fires once even if `navigator.onLine` is unreliable (allowing Service Worker cache hits), and only pauses subsequent retries when offline.

tanstack-query.title: 31. Why is QueryCache.onError preferred over component-level useEffect for global error toasts, and how does `meta` help?
tanstack-query.content: QueryCache({ onError }) fires once per failed query fetch rather than once per subscribed component observer, and `query.meta` lets individual queries attach custom context.

blocks.text:
• The Multi-Observer Toast Bug: Putting `useEffect(() => { if (error) toast(...) }, [error])` inside a shared hook fires N duplicate toasts if N components mount that hook.
• Centralized `QueryCache` / `MutationCache`: Global `onError` callbacks fire exactly once per failed execution.
• Contextual `meta`: Pass `meta: { errorMessage: 'Failed to load billing' }` on specific queries so the global handler can customize alerts or skip silenced queries.

tanstack-query.title: 32. How do you globally customize the default `error` type across all hooks in TanStack Query v5?
tanstack-query.content: Augment the `Register` interface inside `@tanstack/react-query` (`defaultError: ApiError`) via TypeScript declaration merging so every query and mutation infers your custom error class.

blocks.text:
• Default `Error` Type: In v5, `TError` defaults to `Error` (changed from `unknown` in v4).
• Module Augmentation: Declaring `interface Register { defaultError: ApiError }` in a `.d.ts` or shared TS file overrides the default globally.
• Benefit: `error.status` is immediately typed in every `useQuery`, `useMutation`, and `QueryCache` callback without repeating generics everywhere.

tanstack-query.title: 33. What are the essential best practices for unit/integration testing components that use TanStack Query?
tanstack-query.content: Create a fresh isolated QueryClient per test, set `retry: false` so error tests fail fast without timeouts, and mock HTTP at the network boundary (e.g., MSW) rather than mocking `useQuery` itself.

blocks.text:
• Isolated `QueryClient` per Test: Prevents cache leakage between tests.
• `retry: false`: By default, a failing query retries 3 times (~7 seconds), causing test timeouts before error states appear.
• `gcTime: Infinity` in Jest/Vitest: Prevents 'Jest did not exit one second after test run' / open timer warnings.
• Mock Network, Not Hooks: Use MSW or mock fetchers so you test real caching, keys, and state transitions.

tanstack-query.title: 34. How do you persist QueryCache across browser reloads, and what must `gcTime` be set to?
tanstack-query.content: Use `PersistQueryClientProvider` with a storage persister (localStorage/IndexedDB), and ensure `gcTime` is at least equal to `maxAge` (e.g., 24 hours) so persisted entries aren't garbage-collected right after restoration.

blocks.text:
• Persistence Packages: `@tanstack/react-query-persist-client` plus `@tanstack/query-sync-storage-persister` (localStorage) or `@tanstack/query-async-storage-persister` (IndexedDB/AsyncStorage).
• Critical `gcTime` Gotcha: The default `gcTime` is 5 minutes. If a user returns 2 hours later, restored queries older than 5 minutes get garbage-collected immediately unless `gcTime >= maxAge`!
• Cache Busting: Pass `buster: APP_VERSION` to `persistOptions` to discard incompatible persisted schemas on new deployments.

tanstack-query.title: 35. What is the safest way to clear TanStack Query state on user logout or account switching?
tanstack-query.content: Cancel in-flight queries and call `queryClient.clear()` (plus clear any storage persisters) on logout so private data from the previous user never leaks to the next session.

blocks.text:
• Why `invalidateQueries` Isn't Enough: `invalidateQueries()` keeps stale private data visible in memory while refetching (which may fail with 401 and leave stale data around) and retains inactive cache entries.
• Safe Sequence:
  1. `await queryClient.cancelQueries()` so in-flight responses for User A don't land in cache after logout.
  2. `queryClient.clear()` to purge `QueryCache` and `MutationCache` completely.
  3. If using persistence, also remove the persisted storage key.

tanstack-query.title: 36. How does v5's useMutationState() improve on useIsMutating() for cross-component mutation tracking?
tanstack-query.content: useIsMutating() only returns a numeric count of active mutations, whereas useMutationState() subscribes to matching MutationCache entries and lets you select their variables, data, or errors anywhere in the tree.

blocks.text:
• `useIsMutating`: Great for a global spinner (`isMutating > 0`).
• `useMutationState` (New in v5): Subscribes to `MutationCache` using `filters` (`mutationKey`, `status`, `exact`) and `select`.
• Killer Use Case: A mutation triggered inside a modal or row item can be observed in a completely separate sibling list or status bar to render optimistic items or upload progress without lifting state or prop drilling.

tanstack-query.title: 37. How do focusManager and onlineManager work, and how do you integrate them in non-browser environments like React Native?
tanstack-query.content: focusManager and onlineManager abstract window focus and network connectivity events; in React Native, override their event listeners with AppState and NetInfo.

blocks.text:
• Browser Defaults: In web browsers, `focusManager` listens to `visibilitychange` and `onlineManager` listens to `online`/`offline` window events.
• Non-DOM Platforms: React Native lacks `window.visibilitychange`. Wiring `AppState` to `focusManager.setEventListener` and `@react-native-community/netinfo` to `onlineManager.setEventListener` restores automatic background refetches and offline mutation pausing.

tanstack-query.title: 38. Summarize the major breaking changes when migrating from TanStack Query v4 to v5.
tanstack-query.content: v5 mandates a single-object API, removes `onSuccess`/`onError`/`onSettled` from `useQuery`, renames `cacheTime` to `gcTime`, replaces `loading` with `pending`, and replaces `keepPreviousData` with `placeholderData`.

blocks.text:
• Top v4 -> v5 Breaking Changes:
  1. Single object signature only (`useQuery({ queryKey, queryFn })`).
  2. Removed `onSuccess`/`onError`/`onSettled` on `useQuery` (caused duplicate calls per observer and stale closure bugs; move to `QueryCache` or `useMutation`).
  3. `cacheTime` -> `gcTime`, `status: 'loading'` -> `'pending'` (`isPending`), `isInitialLoading` -> `isLoading`.
  4. `useErrorBoundary` -> `throwOnError`.
  5. `keepPreviousData: true` -> `placeholderData: keepPreviousData`.
  6. `useInfiniteQuery` requires `initialPageParam`.

tanstack-query.title: 39. Why were onSuccess, onError, and onSettled callbacks removed from useQuery in v5?
tanstack-query.content: They fired once per component observer rather than once per fetch, didn't fire when reading cached data, and encouraged anti-patterns like copying server state into `useState`.

blocks.text:
• Three Core Reasons:
  1. Multiple Observers = Multiple Executions: Two components using the same hook fired `onSuccess` twice for one HTTP call.
  2. Cache Hits Skipped It: If data was already cached and fresh, `onSuccess` wouldn't run, breaking imperative assumptions.
  3. State Duplication Anti-Pattern: Developers used `onSuccess: (d) => setLocalState(d)` which broke synchronization on background refetches.
• Replacements: Derive values during render, use `select`, pass `values` prop to form libraries (e.g., React Hook Form), or use `QueryCache` callbacks for global alerts.

tanstack-query.title: 40. How do you seed a detail query from an existing list cache using `initialData` and `initialDataUpdatedAt`?
tanstack-query.content: Pass a function to `initialData` that searches the list cache, and pair it with `initialDataUpdatedAt` from `getQueryState` so `staleTime` is evaluated against when the list was actually fetched.

blocks.text:
• Instant Detail Transitions: When clicking a row in a cached list, the detail page renders immediately without a spinner.
• Why `initialDataUpdatedAt` Matters: Without it, TanStack Query assumes `initialData` was created at `Date.now()`! If `staleTime` is 5 minutes, it would skip fetching full details even if the list cache is 4 minutes old.
• Passing `getQueryState(['posts'])?.dataUpdatedAt` accurately reflects the age of the seeded data.

tanstack-query.title: 41. Design a scalable Query Key Factory and explain why hierarchical keys make invalidation surgical.
tanstack-query.content: A Query Key Factory centralizes `as const` key hierarchies from broad scopes (`all`, `lists`) to specific entries (`detail(id)`), preventing typos and enabling granular prefix invalidation.

blocks.text:
• Granular Invalidation Levels:
  - `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.all })`: Invalidates every order list AND detail.
  - `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.lists() })`: Invalidates all filtered lists while preserving cached individual details.
  - `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.detail('123') })`: Targets only one order.
• Tip: Combine with `queryOptions()` in v5 for full type-safe factories.

tanstack-query.title: 42. Why does hydrated SSR data immediately refetch on client mount if `staleTime` stays at its default `0`?
tanstack-query.content: With `staleTime: 0`, hydrated SSR data is immediately considered stale as soon as the client component mounts, triggering a redundant client-side HTTP request right after hydration.

blocks.text:
• The Double-Fetch Trap: The server renders HTML using prefetched data at T=0ms. At T=150ms, React hydrates on the client and mounts `useQuery`. Because `staleTime` defaults to `0`, TanStack Query sees `dataUpdatedAt < now` and fires a duplicate request!
• Fix: Set a positive default `staleTime` (e.g., `60 * 1000`) on your SSR `QueryClient` factory so the client trusts server-hydrated data for the first minute.

tanstack-query.title: 43. How does TanStack Query compare to SWR and RTK Query when choosing a data-fetching layer?
tanstack-query.content: TanStack Query offers richer cache primitives (mutations, optimistic rollbacks, infinite maxPages, Devtools, framework adapters) than SWR and avoids Redux coupling unlike RTK Query.

blocks.text:
• vs. SWR: SWR is minimal and lightweight for simple GET revalidation, whereas TanStack Query provides built-in `gcTime`, mutation tracking (`useMutationState`), `maxPages` bi-directional infinite queries, offline persistence, and `queryOptions`.
• vs. RTK Query: RTK Query excels if your app is already standardized on Redux Toolkit and OpenAPI codegen inside one Redux store. TanStack Query is transport-agnostic (REST, GraphQL, RPC, IndexedDB) and requires zero Redux boilerplate.

tanstack-query.title: 44. Why does queryClient.fetchQuery({ queryKey, queryFn }) default to staleTime: 0 even if you pass initial cache data, and how does ensureQueryData fix this?
tanstack-query.content: fetchQuery calls query.isStaleByTime(options.staleTime ?? 0); if staleTime is omitted, it treats cached data as immediately stale and always hits the network, whereas ensureQueryData returns existing queryData immediately if !== undefined unless revalidateIfStale: true is passed.

blocks.text:
• The `fetchQuery` Trap: Developers often assume `queryClient.fetchQuery({ queryKey })` reads from cache if data exists. In reality, if you don't pass a positive `staleTime` (or configure a global `defaultOptions.queries.staleTime`), `isStaleByTime(0)` is true and `fetchQuery` triggers a network fetch every time.
• How `ensureQueryData` Works: `ensureQueryData` first reads `const cachedData = this.getQueryData(options.queryKey)`. If `cachedData !== undefined`, it returns `Promise.resolve(cachedData)` immediately (and in v5, if `revalidateIfStale: true`, kicks off `prefetchQuery` in the background while still returning cached data synchronously).

tanstack-query.title: 45. What happens if you mutate the oldData argument directly inside queryClient.setQueryData(key, oldData => ...) instead of returning a new clone?
tanstack-query.content: Query.setData runs replaceEqualDeep(this.state.data, newData); if you mutate oldData in-place and return the same reference, replaceEqualDeep sees prev === next, skips reference replacement, and QueryObserver's tracked property diff fails to re-render subscribed components.

blocks.text:
• Reference Identity Contract: Inside `Query.setData(newData, options)`, TanStack Query computes `const data = replaceEqualDeep(this.state.data, newData)`. When you mutate `oldData` in place (`oldData.push(item); return oldData`), `this.state.data === newData` is already `true`.
• Missed Component Re-renders: Because `prevResult.data === nextResult.data`, `QueryObserver.updateResult()` concludes that the tracked `'data'` property has not changed and suppresses calling `useSyncExternalStore` listeners.
• Controlling `updatedAt`: `setQueryData(key, updater, { updatedAt })` also accepts an optional third argument `{ updatedAt: number }` if you need to backdate seeded data so it follows the parent payload's server timestamp.

tanstack-query.title: 46. What is the difference between staleTime: Infinity and staleTime: 'static' in TanStack Query v5?
tanstack-query.content: With staleTime: Infinity, calling invalidateQueries still marks the query stale and refetches it; with staleTime: 'static', query.isStale() permanently returns false even after invalidateQueries(), so the query never refetches again.

blocks.text:
• `staleTime: Infinity`: Data is never stale *by time* (`isStaleByTime(Infinity)` is false), preventing window-focus, mount, and reconnect refetches. However, calling `queryClient.invalidateQueries()` sets `query.state.isInvalidated = true`, which overrides `staleTime: Infinity` and triggers a refetch.
• `staleTime: 'static'` (Added in v5.61+): Designed for true immutable compile-time/boot-time constants or feature flags that must NEVER refetch during the session—even if a broad `queryClient.invalidateQueries()` (with no filter) is executed elsewhere in the app.

tanstack-query.title: 47. What exact properties are passed inside QueryFunctionContext to queryFn(context) in TanStack Query v5?
tanstack-query.content: QueryFunctionContext provides { client, queryKey, signal, meta, pageParam, direction }—where client (added in v5) gives direct access to QueryClient inside standalone queryOptions without closing over external variables.

blocks.text:
• `queryKey`: The readonly typed tuple array passed to `useQuery`, allowing reusable `queryFn` definitions without closure variables.
• `signal`: The lazy `AbortSignal` getter tied to the active `Retryer` and observer lifecycle.
• `client` (New in v5): The `QueryClient` instance executing the fetch—enabling side-cache seeding (`client.setQueryData`) or dependent lookups right inside a static `queryOptions` file.
• `meta`, `pageParam`, `direction`: Custom metadata object, plus infinite query pagination cursor and direction (`'forward' | 'backward'`).

tanstack-query.title: 48. How does the functional form throwOnError: (error, query) => boolean let you distinguish between fatal initial load errors and non-fatal background refetch errors?
tanstack-query.content: Passing throwOnError: (error, query) => query.state.data === undefined && error.status >= 500 throws to the ErrorBoundary only when no cached data exists or on 5xx server crashes, while letting background 4xx/network hiccups fail gracefully in-place.

blocks.text:
• The Danger of `throwOnError: true`: If a user is actively reading a loaded page (`query.state.data !== undefined`) and a background window-focus refetch fails due to a temporary 502 gateway timeout, `throwOnError: true` destroys the entire visible UI and replaces it with the ErrorBoundary fallback.
• Inspecting `query.state.data`: By checking `typeof query.state.data === 'undefined'`, you mimic `useSuspenseQuery`'s default behavior—only escalating to an ErrorBoundary when there is nothing in cache to show the user.

tanstack-query.title: 49. Why can structuralSharing degrade main-thread frame rates on 10,000-row datasets, and how do you profile and tune it?
tanstack-query.content: replaceEqualDeep traverses every nested key of oldData and newData synchronously on the main thread when a query resolves; for payloads with tens of thousands of objects, disabling structuralSharing: false avoids O(N) deep-walk CPU spikes.

blocks.text:
• Synchronous Main-Thread Cost: Every time `Query.setData` runs, `replaceEqualDeep` performs a full depth-first traversal of the JSON tree. For 10,000 rows × 20 columns (200,000 property comparisons), this can block the main thread for 15–40ms.
• When It's Wasted Work: If an analytics endpoint returns a completely new matrix every time or your chart component re-renders the whole canvas anyway, deep reference preservation yields zero benefit.
• Tuning Strategy: Set `structuralSharing: false` on massive list/analytics queries, or use a custom `structuralSharing` function that compares row IDs/version hashes in `O(rows)` without recursing into every column.

tanstack-query.title: 50. How does infiniteQueryOptions() complement queryOptions() in TanStack Query v5 for sharing paginated cache configurations?
tanstack-query.content: infiniteQueryOptions() brands the queryKey with InfiniteData<TQueryFnData, TPageParam> so useInfiniteQuery, useSuspenseInfiniteQuery, prefetchInfiniteQuery, and setQueryData infer the { pages, pageParams } structure automatically.

blocks.text:
• Type Branding for `{ pages, pageParams }`: Unlike a regular query where cache data equals `TQueryFnData`, an infinite query stores `InfiniteData<TData, TPageParam>` (`{ pages: TData[], pageParams: TPageParam[] }`) in `QueryCache`.
• Preventing Shape Corruption: By branding `options.queryKey` with `DataTag<TQueryKey, InfiniteData<TQueryFnData, TPageParam>>`, calling `queryClient.setQueryData(feedInfiniteOptions().queryKey, updater)` enforces that your `updater` returns `{ pages, pageParams }` rather than a single page.

tanstack-query.title: 51. How does useSuspenseQueries() execute dynamic parallel Suspense queries without causing a request waterfall?
tanstack-query.content: useSuspenseQueries fires all underlying query fetches simultaneously before throwing the first pending Promise to React Suspense, ensuring every network request is already in-flight in QueryCache while the boundary is suspended.

blocks.text:
• Parallel Eager Initiation: Unlike sequential `useSuspenseQuery` calls where the first `throw promise` aborts the component render before line 2 executes, `useSuspenseQueries({ queries: [...] })` receives the entire array of query definitions upfront.
• Non-Nullable Output Tuple: Once all queries in the array resolve, `useSuspenseQueries` returns results where every item's `data` property is guaranteed to be defined (`TData`, never `undefined`).

tanstack-query.title: 52. How do you prefetch multiple initial pages of an infinite query on the server or hover using prefetchInfiniteQuery in v5?
tanstack-query.content: In TanStack Query v5, prefetchInfiniteQuery accepts a pages: number option alongside getNextPageParam to sequentially prefetch N pages into QueryCache before rendering or dehydrating.

blocks.text:
• Multi-Page Server Prefetching: If a user deep-links to a feed or you want the initial SSR HTML to include the first 3 pages of a catalog, v5 allows passing `pages: 3` to `queryClient.prefetchInfiniteQuery`.
• How It Works Internally: `prefetchInfiniteQuery` loops `pages` times, calling `getNextPageParam(lastPage, allPages, lastPageParam, allPageParams)` after each resolved page, and stops early if `getNextPageParam` returns `undefined` or `null`.

tanstack-query.title: 53. Why should PWAs using Service Worker HTTP caching or local IndexedDB interceptors use networkMode: 'offlineFirst' instead of 'online' or 'always'?
tanstack-query.content: networkMode: 'offlineFirst' executes the first queryFn call immediately even when navigator.onLine is false (allowing the Service Worker cache to respond), and only pauses subsequent retry attempts if that initial request fails.

blocks.text:
• Why `'online'` Fails PWAs: In default `'online'` mode, if `onlineManager.isOnline()` is `false`, `Retryer` pauses *before* calling `queryFn` even once—meaning your Service Worker cache or local Cache API is never even asked for the resource!
• Why `'always'` Fails PWAs: In `'always'` mode, `queryFn` runs immediately, but if the asset is *not* in the Service Worker cache and throws a network error, `'always'` immediately burns through all 3 retries and transitions to `status: 'error'` while offline.
• The `'offlineFirst'` Sweet Spot: Runs `queryFn` attempt #1 immediately (hitting Service Worker cache if available); if attempt #1 rejects because it needed the real network, it pauses retry #1 (`fetchStatus: 'paused'`) until connectivity returns.

tanstack-query.title: 54. How do you enforce strict TypeScript types on query.meta and mutation.meta globally across your application?
tanstack-query.content: Extend the Register interface inside declare module '@tanstack/react-query' with queryMeta: MyQueryMeta and mutationMeta: MyMutationMeta so every useQuery, useMutation, and QueryCache callback gets autocomplete and compile-time validation.

blocks.text:
• Default `Record<string, unknown>`: Out of the box, `meta` is loosely typed as `Record<string, unknown> | undefined`, making typos like `meta: { errorMassage: '...' }` silent bugs.
• Module Augmentation via `Register`: Just like `defaultError`, TanStack Query v5 exposes `queryMeta` and `mutationMeta` hooks on the `Register` interface.
• End-to-End Safety: Once augmented, passing an invalid property to `meta` in `useQuery`, `queryOptions`, `useMutation`, or reading `query.meta` in `QueryCache.onError` is strictly type-checked.

tanstack-query.title: 55. What is the exact behavioral difference between invalidateQueries({ refetchType: 'all' }) and refetchQueries({ type: 'all' })?
tanstack-query.content: invalidateQueries first marks matching queries as invalidated (state.isInvalidated = true) before refetching, whereas refetchQueries triggers an immediate network fetch without marking the query invalidated and skips queries that have enabled: false.

blocks.text:
• Why `invalidateQueries` is Safer: If an inactive query has no mounted observers (`refetchType: 'active'` by default), `invalidateQueries` flips `state.isInvalidated = true` without wasting a network request right now. When the user visits that screen 2 minutes later, it automatically refetches on mount.
• What `refetchQueries` Does: It does NOT set `isInvalidated = true`; it immediately executes `query.fetch()` on matching queries. Furthermore, if a query has `gcTime` elapsed or no `queryFn` attached yet, `refetchQueries` cannot mark future mounts stale.

tanstack-query.title: 56. What does the useIsRestoring() hook return, and how does useBaseQuery use it internally during offline cache restoration?
tanstack-query.content: useIsRestoring() reads IsRestoringContext provided by PersistQueryClientProvider; while true, useBaseQuery suppresses observer.setOptions fetch side-effects and forces fetchStatus: 'idle' so components wait for async storage hydration instead of firing premature network requests.

blocks.text:
• The Async Storage Race Condition: IndexedDB and React Native `AsyncStorage` are asynchronous. When the app mounts on frame 1, `QueryCache` is empty while the storage read is in-flight.
• How `isRestoring` Blocks Network Stamps: Inside `useBaseQuery`, if `isRestoring` is `true`, the hook skips running the `useEffect` that triggers initial fetches and returns an optimistic result with `fetchStatus: 'idle'` and `isPending: true`.
• Automatic Flush: Once the storage promise resolves and `hydrate()` populates `QueryCache`, `PersistQueryClientProvider` flips `isRestoring` to `false`, causing all mounted queries to render the restored data or revalidate if stale.

tanstack-query.title: 57. How does queryClient.resetQueries() differ from removeQueries() when a query was initialized with initialData?
tanstack-query.content: removeQueries deletes the Query instance completely from QueryCache (notifying observers with undefined), whereas resetQueries resets the Query's state back to its initial state (preserving initialData if provided) and immediately refetches active observers.

blocks.text:
• `query.reset()` State Restoration: Calling `queryClient.resetQueries({ queryKey })` invokes `query.reset()` on each matching `Query`, restoring `state` back to `#initialState` (which evaluates `options.initialData` if configured, or `status: 'pending', data: undefined` otherwise).
• Active Refetching: After resetting the state, `resetQueries` automatically calls `refetchQueries` on all active (mounted) matching queries.
• `removeQueries`: Evicts the `Query` from the `QueryCache` map without triggering a refetch, which can leave mounted components in an orphaned state until their next re-render.

tanstack-query.title: 58. Compare the two optimistic update patterns in TanStack Query v5: UI-level variables vs. Cache-level onMutate rollback.
tanstack-query.content: UI-level optimistic updates render `mutation.variables` directly while `isPending` (zero cache rollback code), while cache-level updates write to QueryCache in `onMutate` and restore snapshots in `onError`.

blocks.text:
• Pattern 1 — UI-Level (v5 simplified): Keep `useMutation` simple with `onSettled: () => invalidateQueries(...)`, then render `isPending ? [...todos, variables] : todos` in the single component displaying the mutation. No `onMutate` or manual rollback needed.
• Pattern 2 — Cache-Level (`onMutate`): Required when multiple components across the tree must reflect the optimistic change immediately.
  1. `await cancelQueries` to prevent stale in-flight refetches from overwriting the optimistic write.
  2. Snapshot `getQueryData` and return it as context.
  3. Roll back in `onError` using `context`, and always `invalidateQueries` in `onSettled`.

tanstack-query.title: 59. What happens if a user triggers two rapid optimistic mutations on the same list, and how do you prevent flickering?
tanstack-query.content: If the first mutation's `onSettled` invalidates the list before the second mutation finishes on the server, the refetch can overwrite the second optimistic item; guard invalidation with `queryClient.isMutating()`.

blocks.text:
• The Concurrency Bug: User toggles Todo A then immediately toggles Todo B. Mutation A finishes first and calls `invalidateQueries(['todos'])`. Because Mutation B hasn't committed on the server yet, the refetch returns stale state for B, reverting B's optimistic toggle temporarily.
• Fix: Tag related mutations with `mutationKey: ['todos']` and inside `onSettled`, only invalidate when `queryClient.isMutating({ mutationKey: ['todos'] }) === 1` (or `<= 1` depending on phase), ensuring the final settled mutation triggers the authoritative refetch.

tanstack-query.title: 60. How does refetching work for useInfiniteQuery, and how does maxPages control memory?
tanstack-query.content: Invalidating an infinite query sequentially refetches every currently loaded page from page 1 using stored pageParams; `maxPages` bounds the stored page window and evicts distant pages.

blocks.text:
• Sequential Page Refetch: Unlike regular queries, refetching an infinite query with 10 loaded pages sequentially re-runs `queryFn` for all 10 stored `pageParams` (so mutations don't leave holes). Note: `refetchPage` was removed in v5 in favor of `maxPages`.
• `maxPages`: Caps the number of pages stored in `data.pages`. Fetching page 6 when `maxPages: 5` drops page 1; scrolling back up uses `getPreviousPageParam` and `fetchPreviousPage` to reload earlier pages on demand.

tanstack-query.title: 61. How does useSuspenseQuery differ from useQuery, and what waterfall pitfall should you avoid with Suspense?
tanstack-query.content: useSuspenseQuery suspends rendering until resolved, throws errors to Error Boundaries, and guarantees non-undefined `data`; however, two consecutive useSuspenseQuery calls in one component create a request waterfall.

blocks.text:
• Key Differences from `useQuery`:
  1. `data` is never `undefined`—loading states move to `<Suspense>` and errors move to `<ErrorBoundary>`.
  2. `enabled` and `placeholderData` are disallowed (use conditional rendering or `useSuspenseQueries`).
• Waterfall Trap: Calling `useSuspenseQuery(A)` then `useSuspenseQuery(B)` in the same component suspends on A before B even starts!
• Solutions: Batch independent queries with `useSuspenseQueries`, or prefetch both queries ahead of render (e.g., in a route loader or parent component).

tanstack-query.title: 62. How do dehydrate() and HydrationBoundary work in SSR (e.g., Next.js App Router), and why create QueryClient per request on the server?
tanstack-query.content: dehydrate() serializes QueryCache entries into JSON-safe dehydrated state for HydrationBoundary on the client; creating one QueryClient per server request prevents cross-user data leaks.

blocks.text:
• Request Isolation Security: A module-level singleton `QueryClient` on a Node.js server would share User A's private data with User B! Always instantiate a fresh `QueryClient` per SSR request.
• Client Singleton vs. State: On the client, keep one `QueryClient` across the browser session (via `useState` or a browser-only singleton gated by `isServer`).
• `dehydrate` + `HydrationBoundary`: `dehydrate(serverClient)` extracts successful (and optionally pending in v5.40+) queries into props; `HydrationBoundary` merges them into the browser `QueryClient` before client hooks read them.

tanstack-query.title: 63. How can TanStack Query v5 stream in-flight server queries to the client without awaiting prefetchQuery on the server?
tanstack-query.content: By configuring `shouldDehydrateQuery` to include `status === 'pending'`, Next.js Server Components can fire `prefetchQuery` without `await` and stream the Promise resolution directly into HydrationBoundary.

blocks.text:
• Traditional Blocking SSR: `await queryClient.prefetchQuery(...)` delays the HTML shell until the slow API finishes.
• Streaming Pending Queries: In Next.js App Router, omit `await` on `queryClient.prefetchQuery(...)` and allow `status === 'pending'` inside `shouldDehydrateQuery`.
• Result: The server sends the shell immediately, keeps the promise alive, and streams the resolved query payload to the client `HydrationBoundary` seamlessly.

tanstack-query.title: 64. How do tracked properties and `notifyOnChangeProps` minimize re-renders in TanStack Query?
tanstack-query.content: By default, TanStack Query tracks which result properties your component destructures (`data`, `isFetching`, `error`) via getters and only re-renders when those accessed properties change.

blocks.text:
• Tracked Queries (Default since v4): The object returned from `useQuery` defines property getters. If your component only reads `data`, background refetches that flip `isFetching` from `false` to `true` and back will NOT trigger re-renders unless `data` actually changed.
• Pitfall: Spreading the entire result (`const query = useQuery(...); console.log({ ...query })`) accesses every getter and opts out of tracking.
• `notifyOnChangeProps: 'all'` disables tracking if you intentionally need updates on every state transition.

tanstack-query.title: 65. How should you integrate WebSockets or Server-Sent Events (SSE) with TanStack Query?
tanstack-query.content: Keep initial fetching in `useQuery` with a high `staleTime`, and inside a WebSocket listener either push full payloads via `setQueryData` or send lightweight invalidation signals via `invalidateQueries`.

blocks.text:
• Two Integration Strategies:
  1. Event-Driven Invalidation (Simplest & Most Resilient): Server pushes `{ type: 'invalidate', entity: 'orders' }`; client calls `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] })`.
  2. Direct Cache Patching: Server pushes the full updated object; client merges it with `queryClient.setQueryData` and sets `staleTime: Infinity` on the query so redundant HTTP polls don't fire.
• Reconnection Safety: On WebSocket reconnect after a drop, call `invalidateQueries` to catch up on missed events.

tanstack-query.title: 66. How do QueryClient, QueryCache, Query, and QueryObserver interact under the hood in TanStack Query?
tanstack-query.content: QueryClient is the imperative facade over QueryCache, which stores singleton Query instances keyed by queryHash; each mounted useQuery creates a QueryObserver that subscribes to one Query and projects options-filtered results to React.

blocks.text:
• QueryClient: The top-level controller used by application code (`prefetchQuery`, `invalidateQueries`, `setQueryData`) and holder of default options.
• QueryCache: An in-memory `Map<queryHash, Query>` that emits global cache lifecycle events and owns garbage collection.
• Query: The state machine holding raw `state` (`data`, `error`, `status`, `fetchStatus`, `dataUpdatedAt`), the active `Retryer`, and a `Set<QueryObserver>`.
• QueryObserver: Created per `useQuery` hook call; applies local options (`select`, `staleTime`, `placeholderData`, `notifyOnChangeProps`) and notifies its specific React component.

tanstack-query.title: 67. How does useQuery bridge QueryObserver to React's rendering lifecycle using useSyncExternalStore?
tanstack-query.content: useBaseQuery instantiates a stable QueryObserver in a ref/state and passes observer.subscribe and observer.getCurrentResult to React's useSyncExternalStore to prevent tearing in concurrent renders.

blocks.text:
• Concurrent Safety: TanStack Query v5 lives outside React state inside `QueryCache`, so it uses React 18's `useSyncExternalStore` to synchronize external cache mutations safely.
• Subscription Function: `useCallback((onStoreChange) => observer.subscribe(notifyManager.batchCalls(onStoreChange)), [observer])` registers the component listener on mount and removes it on unmount.
• Snapshot Getter: `() => observer.getCurrentResult()` returns the memoized observer result reference; React only triggers a re-render if `Object.is(prevSnapshot, nextSnapshot)` becomes false.

tanstack-query.title: 68. How does TanStack Query's deterministic hashKey algorithm serialize queryKeys internally?
tanstack-query.content: hashKey uses JSON.stringify with a custom replacer that clones plain objects with lexicographically sorted keys while preserving array indices, producing identical queryHash strings regardless of object property insertion order.

blocks.text:
• Plain Object Normalization: Inside `hashKey(queryKey)`, the JSON replacer checks `isPlainObject(val)`. If true, `Object.keys(val).sort()` builds a new object with keys in alphabetical order.
• Array Order Preservation: Arrays are not sorted by the replacer, so `['todos', 1, 2]` and `['todos', 2, 1]` produce completely different `queryHash` strings.
• Custom `queryKeyHashFn`: If your `queryKey` contains `Map`, `Set`, `BigInt`, or class instances that `JSON.stringify` drops or throws on, you can supply a custom `queryKeyHashFn` in `QueryClient` defaultOptions.

tanstack-query.title: 69. How does replaceEqualDeep(prevData, nextData) work internally, and why does it skip non-plain objects?
tanstack-query.content: replaceEqualDeep recursively walks plain arrays and plain objects, counting equal children; if all elements match, it returns the exact previous reference, and it bails out on Date/Map/Set/class instances to avoid corrupting prototypes.

blocks.text:
• Short-circuit Equality: If `a === b`, it immediately returns `a`.
• Recursive Child Counting: It iterates over the union of keys/indices, calling `replaceEqualDeep(a[key], b[key])`, and increments `equalItems` whenever the returned child reference `=== a[key]`.
• Parent Reference Reuse: If `aSize === bSize && equalItems === aSize`, it returns `a` instead of the newly constructed clone `copy`, preserving referential identity up the tree.
• Non-Plain Guard: If neither side is a plain array or `isPlainObject`, it returns `b` directly so `Date`, `RegExp`, `Map`, or custom classes are replaced as-is.

tanstack-query.title: 70. How does QueryObserver track accessed properties via JavaScript Getters/Proxies, and why does object rest spread break it?
tanstack-query.content: QueryObserver wraps getOptimisticResult in an object with custom property getters that record every accessed key into trackedProps; spreading or logging the whole result object accesses every key and subscribes the component to all state transitions.

blocks.text:
• Getter Instrumentation: In `observer.trackResult(result)`, TanStack Query defines custom `Object.defineProperty` getters for every field (`data`, `error`, `isFetching`, `status`, etc.).
• Lazy Subscription Set: Reading `result.data` pushes `'data'` into `this.#trackedProps`. On the next cache notification, the observer checks if any property in `#trackedProps` changed (`prevResult[key] !== nextResult[key]`).
• The Rest/Spread Trap: Writing `const { data, ...rest } = useQuery(...)` enumerates all enumerable properties on the result object, invoking every getter and adding `isFetching`, `dataUpdatedAt`, and `fetchStatus` to `#trackedProps`.

tanstack-query.title: 71. How many valid combinations exist in TanStack Query's orthogonal (status × fetchStatus) state machine, and what triggers each transition?
tanstack-query.content: The 3 data statuses ('pending', 'success', 'error') cross with 3 network statuses ('fetching', 'paused', 'idle') to form 9 orthogonal states that cleanly model initial loads, offline pauses, background refetches, and soft errors.

blocks.text:
• `pending` × (`fetching` | `paused` | `idle`): Initial fetch in flight (`isLoading: true`), initial fetch waiting for network reconnection, or disabled query (`enabled: false`) with no cache data.
• `success` × (`fetching` | `paused` | `idle`): Background refetch while displaying stale data (`isRefetching: true`), queued background revalidate while offline, or settled fresh/stale data in cache.
• `error` × (`fetching` | `paused` | `idle`): Manual/automatic refetch of a previously failed query, paused retry after error, or terminal error state after retries exhaust.

tanstack-query.title: 72. How does Removable manage the gcTime garbage-collection timer and observer reference counting inside a Query instance?
tanstack-query.content: Query inherits from Removable; when the last QueryObserver unsubscribes (observers.length === 0), scheduleGc() starts a setTimeout for gcTime that calls queryCache.remove(this) unless a new observer mounts and calls clearGcTimeout().

blocks.text:
• Max `gcTime` Wins: Each `QueryObserver` calls `query.updateGcTime(options.gcTime)`, and the `Query` stores `Math.max(this.gcTime || 0, newGcTime)` so the longest observer retention policy prevails.
• Active vs. Inactive Transition: `addObserver()` immediately calls `clearGcTimeout()`. When `removeObserver()` drops `this.observers.length` to `0`, it invokes `scheduleGc()`.
• Node.js / Infinity Guard: If `gcTime` is `Infinity` or exceeds browser max 32-bit signed integer (`2147483647` ms ≈ 24.8 days), `scheduleGc()` skips scheduling `setTimeout` to prevent immediate overflow execution.

tanstack-query.title: 73. How does TanStack Query's internal Retryer class orchestrate retries, pause/continue on network loss, and request deduplication?
tanstack-query.content: Query.fetch stores an active #retryer instance; concurrent fetch calls return this.#retryer.promise while the Retryer recursive loop manages attempt counts, backoff sleep timers, onlineManager pause hooks, and cancellation.

blocks.text:
• Single Flight Promise: When `query.fetch()` runs while `this.state.fetchStatus !== 'idle'` and `this.#retryer` exists, it reuses `this.#retryer.promise` instead of invoking `fn()` again.
• Loop & Sleep Mechanics: On failure, `Retryer` calculates `shouldRetry` and `delay`, dispatches a `failed` action to update `failureCount` and `failureReason`, sleeps for `delay`, and checks if the browser went offline.
• Pause & Resume: If `canContinue()` returns false (offline in `online` mode), `Retryer` creates a continuation promise and registers a listener on `onlineManager`/`focusManager` to resume the exact loop step when connectivity returns.

tanstack-query.title: 74. Why does TanStack Query only cancel an in-flight request on unmount if your queryFn explicitly reads the signal property?
tanstack-query.content: Query.fetch defines signal as a lazy JavaScript getter on QueryFunctionContext that sets abortSignalConsumed = true when read; on last observer unmount, Query only calls abortController.abort() if abortSignalConsumed is true.

blocks.text:
• Lazy Getter Detection: `addSignalProperty(queryFnContext)` uses `Object.defineProperty(object, 'signal', { enumerable: true, get: () => { abortSignalConsumed = true; return abortController.signal; } })`.
• Why Not Always Abort? If `queryFn` does not forward `signal` to `fetch()` or `axios`, aborting the internal `Retryer` on unmount would discard a network response that is already in-flight and about to resolve into cache.
• Smart Fallback: When `signal` is NOT consumed, TanStack Query lets the network promise finish in the background and populate `QueryCache`. When `signal` IS consumed, unmounting the last observer aborts the HTTP request and reverts `fetchStatus` to `'idle'`.

tanstack-query.title: 75. What is the role of notifyManager in TanStack Query, and how do batch(), batchCalls(), and setScheduler() optimize React updates?
tanstack-query.content: notifyManager queues observer and cache listener callbacks during synchronous transactions (like invalidateQueries matching 50 queries) and flushes them in a single scheduled microtask/React batch.

blocks.text:
• Transaction Counting: `notifyManager.batch(fn)` increments a `#transactions` counter before running `fn()` and decrements it after. While `#transactions > 0`, `schedule(cb)` pushes callbacks to a queue instead of firing immediately.
• Single Flush: Once the outermost `batch()` exits (`#transactions === 0`), `flush()` schedules all queued observer notifications inside `notifyFn` (which `@tanstack/react-query` wires to React's batching).
• Custom Scheduler: `notifyManager.setScheduler(cb => setTimeout(cb, 0))` or `requestAnimationFrame` allows shifting high-frequency cache notifications to custom frame budgets.

tanstack-query.title: 76. How do serial mutation scopes (scope: { id }) work in TanStack Query v5's MutationCache?
tanstack-query.content: Mutations sharing the same scope.id are queued serially by MutationCache: the first executes immediately while subsequent mutations enter status: 'pending' with isPaused: true until the preceding mutation in that scope settles.

blocks.text:
• Why Serial Scopes? Parallel mutations on the same entity (e.g., rapid auto-save edits or reordering items) often arrive out-of-order on the server, causing race conditions.
• Internal Queueing: Before running a mutation, `MutationCache.canRun(mutation)` checks if another mutation with the same `mutation.options.scope?.id` is currently `'pending'` and not paused.
• Automatic Continuation: When the active mutation in a scope settles (succeeds or fails), `MutationCache.resumePausedMutations()` finds the next waiting mutation in that scope and starts its `Retryer`.

tanstack-query.title: 77. Why do callbacks passed to useMutation({ onSuccess }) behave differently on unmount compared to callbacks passed to mutate(vars, { onSuccess })?
tanstack-query.content: useMutation options belong to the Mutation instance in MutationCache and always run even if the component unmounts, whereas mutate() callbacks are registered on the component's MutationObserver and are skipped if the component unmounts or fires mutate() again.

blocks.text:
• `useMutation({ onSuccess, onSettled })`: Executed directly by `Mutation.execute()` inside `MutationCache`. Because the cache outlives React components, cache invalidations placed here are guaranteed to run.
• `mutate(variables, { onSuccess })`: Stored on the `MutationObserver` via `#currentMutation`. When the component unmounts, `observer.onUnmount()` clears listeners, and calling `mutate()` a second time replaces `#currentMutation` on that observer.
• Architectural Rule: Put data/cache logic (`invalidateQueries`) in `useMutation` options, and put component-coupled UI actions (`router.push`, `closeModal`, `resetForm`) in `mutate()` callbacks.

tanstack-query.title: 78. How does useSuspenseQuery integrate with React Suspense under the hood, and when does it throw a Promise vs. an Error?
tanstack-query.content: useBaseQuery checks shouldSuspend(defaultedOptions, result): when status === 'pending', it throws observer.fetchOptimistic(defaultedOptions) (a Promise) to suspend React; when status === 'error' and !isFetching, it throws result.error to the nearest ErrorBoundary.

blocks.text:
• Suspending the Fiber: React Suspense works when a component throws a thenable (`Promise`) during render. `useSuspenseQuery` sets `suspense: true`, `enabled: true` (locked), and `throwOnError: defaultThrowOnError`.
• When `shouldSuspend` is true (`result.isPending`): `useBaseQuery` throws `observer.fetchOptimistic(defaultedOptions)`. React catches the promise, renders the `<Suspense fallback>`, and re-renders the subtree when the query resolves.
• Soft Refetch Errors: Notice `defaultThrowOnError` only throws to the ErrorBoundary if `query.state.data === undefined`. If cached data already exists and a background refetch fails, it retains the stale `data` rather than crashing the already-rendered page.

tanstack-query.title: 79. How does useQueryErrorResetBoundary coordinate between an ErrorBoundary and useBaseQuery to prevent an infinite throw loop on retry?
tanstack-query.content: QueryErrorResetBoundary provides a mutable context Value with an isReset() boolean flag; calling reset() flips isReset to true for the next render pass so getHasError() suppresses re-throwing the old cached error and triggers a fresh fetch instead.

blocks.text:
• The Infinite Loop Problem: When a query fails, `query.state.status` remains `'error'` in `QueryCache`. If an ErrorBoundary simply re-renders its children on 'Try Again', `useSuspenseQuery` sees `status === 'error'` in cache and immediately throws the exact same error again.
• The `isReset()` Handshake: Calling `errorResetBoundary.reset()` sets an internal boolean `isReset = true`. During the next render of `useBaseQuery`, if `errorResetBoundary.isReset()` is true, `getHasError()` returns `false`.
• Consuming the Reset: A `useEffect` in `useBaseQuery` then calls `errorResetBoundary.clearReset()` and triggers `observer.refetch()`, cleanly retrying the network call.

tanstack-query.title: 80. What exact data structure does dehydrate(queryClient) produce, and how does hydrate() reconcile incoming timestamps with existing client cache entries?
tanstack-query.content: dehydrate outputs { mutations, queries: [{ queryKey, queryHash, state, promise? }] }; on the client, hydrate compares incoming state.dataUpdatedAt against existing query.state.dataUpdatedAt and only overwrites the cache if the dehydrated snapshot is newer.

blocks.text:
• Dehydrated Payload: Each `DehydratedQuery` contains `queryKey`, `queryHash`, `state` (`data`, `dataUpdatedAt`, `error`, `status`, `fetchMeta`), and optionally a `promise` when streaming pending queries in v5.
• Timestamp Conflict Resolution: When navigating between SSR routes, the client `QueryCache` may already hold fresher data than the server payload. `hydrate()` checks ` dehydratedQuery.state.dataUpdatedAt > query.state.dataUpdatedAt` before calling `query.setState()`.
• Custom Serialization (`serializeData` / `deserializeData`): In v5, `defaultOptions.dehydrate.serializeData` (e.g., `superjson.serialize`) and `defaultOptions.hydrate.deserializeData` handle rich types across the RSC boundary.

tanstack-query.title: 81. How does <HydrationBoundary> hydrate queries synchronously during render without triggering setState-in-render warnings?
tanstack-query.content: HydrationBoundary hydrates NEW queries immediately during render so child useQuery hooks read populated cache on first pass, while queuing updates for EXISTING observed queries into a ref that flushes inside useEffect after commit.

blocks.text:
• The Render-Phase Challenge: Child components inside `<HydrationBoundary>` call `useQuery()` during the very same render pass. If hydration waited for `useEffect`, children would initially render `isPending: true` and flash a loading state.
• Split Hydration Strategy: Inside `useMemo` during render, `<HydrationBoundary>` checks `queryCache.get(dehydratedQuery.queryHash)`. If the query does NOT exist yet, it calls `hydrate()` immediately because no active `QueryObserver` is subscribed yet.
• Deferred Active Updates: If the query already exists in `QueryCache` (e.g., from a previous client navigation), mutating it during render would notify mounted observers mid-render. Therefore, `<HydrationBoundary>` pushes it to `hydrationQueue` and hydrates it inside `useEffect`.

tanstack-query.title: 82. How are onlineManager and focusManager implemented on top of the Subscribable base class, and how does setEventListener override browser defaults?
tanstack-query.content: Both managers extend Subscribable, maintain a cleanup function #cleanup, attach default window 'online'/'offline' and 'visibilitychange' listeners in browser environments, and notify QueryCache.onOnline() / onFocus() when triggered.

blocks.text:
• Default Browser Events: In v5, `focusManager` listens ONLY to `window.addEventListener('visibilitychange')` (removing legacy `focus` event false-positives from DevTools/alerts), while `onlineManager` listens to `online` and `offline`.
• `setEventListener(setupFn)`: Calling `setEventListener` executes the previous `#cleanup?.()` to detach default DOM listeners, passes a handler callback into your `setupFn`, and stores your returned teardown function as the new `#cleanup`.
• Propagation to Queries: When `focusManager.onFocus()` fires, `QueryClient` iterates `queryCache.getAll()` and `mutationCache.getAll()` inside `notifyManager.batch()`, calling `query.onFocus()` on every active query.

tanstack-query.title: 83. How does persistQueryClient synchronize QueryCache with external storage, and how do buster, maxAge, and gcTime interact during restoration?
tanstack-query.content: persistQueryClient restores persisted dehydrated state via hydrate() before subscribing to QueryCache/MutationCache updates; on restore, if persistedClient.buster !== buster or timestamp exceeds maxAge, it wipes storage instead of hydrating.

blocks.text:
• Expiration & Cache Busting: The persisted envelope stores `{ timestamp, buster, clientState }`. On boot, `persistQueryClientRestore` checks `Date.now() - persistedClient.timestamp > maxAge` or `persistedClient.buster !== buster`; if either fails, it calls `persister.removeClient()`.
• Why `gcTime >= maxAge` is Mandatory: Even if `maxAge` is 24 hours, `hydrate()` restores each query's original `dataUpdatedAt`. If `gcTime` is left at the default 5 minutes, `scheduleGc()` sees the query is inactive and immediately garbage-collects the freshly restored cache.
• Pause/Resume Hydration Lock: Using `<PersistQueryClientProvider>` holds queries in `fetchStatus: 'idle'` until the async storage restoration promise resolves, preventing premature duplicate network requests during IndexedDB reads.

tanstack-query.title: 84. How does QueryObserver memoize the select(data) transformation internally, and what exact conditions cause select to re-execute?
tanstack-query.content: QueryObserver caches #selectData, #selectResult, and #selectFn; it only re-runs options.select(data) if query.state.data !== #selectData or options.select !== #selectFn, and then applies replaceEqualDeep to the selected output.

blocks.text:
• Dual-Reference Check: Inside `QueryObserver.createResult()`, TanStack Query checks `if (options.select && state.data !== undefined)`. If `state.data === this.#selectData && options.select === this.#selectFn`, it reuses `this.#selectResult` without invoking `select`.
• Second-Stage Structural Sharing: When `select` DOES run, its return value is passed through `replaceEqualDeep(this.#selectResult, newSelectedData)`. Thus, even if `state.data` changed (e.g., an unrelated todo item updated) and `select` returned a new object literal `{ count: 5 }`, `replaceEqualDeep` keeps the old `{ count: 5 }` reference!
• Error Isolation: If `options.select(data)` throws an exception, `QueryObserver` catches it into `#selectError` and transitions the observer result to `isError: true` without corrupting the shared `Query` in `QueryCache`.

tanstack-query.title: 85. How does infiniteQueryBehavior() use fetchMeta to distinguish between forward pagination, backward pagination, and full multi-page refetches?
tanstack-query.content: useInfiniteQuery attaches infiniteQueryBehavior() to the Query; fetchNextPage/fetchPreviousPage dispatch fetchMeta: { fetchMore: { direction: 'forward' | 'backward' } } to append/prepend one page, whereas a normal refetch loops sequentially through all existing pages.

blocks.text:
• `onFetch` Hook in QueryBehavior: In `@tanstack/query-core`, `Query` is generic and delegates infinite pagination logic to `infiniteQueryBehavior().onFetch(context, query)`.
• Single-Page Append/Prepend: When `context.fetchOptions?.meta?.fetchMore?.direction` is `'forward'` or `'backward'`, the behavior calls `getNextPageParam` or `getPreviousPageParam`, fetches just that single page, and appends/prepends it (trimming the opposite end if `maxPages` is set).
• Full Sequential Refetch: When `fetchMore` is absent (e.g., window focus refetch or `invalidateQueries`), the behavior iterates from page `0` to `pages.length - 1`, passing each fresh page into `getNextPageParam` to rebuild the entire `{ pages, pageParams }` array consistently.

tanstack-query.title: 86. What does QueryObserver.getOptimisticResult(options) do during React render, and why is it necessary when queryKeys change dynamically?
tanstack-query.content: When props like userId change during render, useBaseQuery calls observer.getOptimisticResult(defaultedOptions) to synchronously resolve the new Query from QueryCache before useEffect runs, preventing a one-frame stale flash of the previous user's data.

blocks.text:
